01 · The ask

Strong enough. With less metal.

DecisionStart from real parts
1What I noticedMe, before any study
Me · what I noticed
A standard part carries metal where no load flows.In a vehicle, that is mass you pay to carry, every mile.What if the solver showed me where to remove it?
Less material

Metal stays only where the load flows.

Lighter parts

Down 59% (pedal) and 52% (clamp) in simulation.

Less fuel

Less self-weight to carry means lower running cost in a vehicle.

Cut part mass without losing strength, as measured by mass and safety factor in simulation, by letting generative design remove material that carries no load

02 · The trade-off

Lighter flexes more. Three calls.

DecisionCheck displacement too
1The trade-offMe, checking my own work
Me · the push-back
Lighter parts flex more.So strength alone is the wrong test.I checked displacement as well as safety factor.
Call 1
Same loads for every version
Why
Parts compared under different conditions prove nothing.
The call
Fix the loads, material and constraints across versions.
What it gives
Differences come from the shape alone.
Call 2
Optimize first, then generate
Why
Jumping to a lattice hides what the part needs.
The call
Shape optimization first, then generative design, with stiffness and weight as goals.
What it gives
Three versions per part: standard, optimized, generative.
Call 3
Check stiffness, not just strength
Why
Lighter parts flex more.
The call
Compare displacement beside safety factor.
What it gives
The trade-off is visible, not hidden.

07 · Takeaways

Four rules from the real part.

Rule 01

Start from the real part

What I saw
A finished component is the honest baseline.
Next time
Measure change against something real.
Rule 02

Remove what carries no load

What I saw
Generative design shows where the part does no work.
Next time
Ask what each piece is doing before keeping it.
Rule 03

Check the trade-off

What I saw
Lighter parts flex more, so strength alone is not enough.
Next time
Test the thing that quietly gets worse.
Rule 04

Make it, test it, fix it

What I saw
The same habit holds on screens, across markets.
Next time
Build the thing, then learn from it.
